Are historic and current hepatitis B viral DNA and quantitative HBsAg level associated with cirrhosis in non-Asian women with chronic hepatitis B?

Tool call input: {'knowledge_bases': ['pubmed_papers'], 'search_rounds_budget': 5, 'search_target': 'Find clinical studies evaluating whether historical/prior and current serum hepatitis B virus DNA levels and quantitative HBsAg (qHBsAg) levels are associated with prevalent cirrhosis among non-Asian women with chronic hepatitis B. Identify the specific cohort/population, adjusted associations and direction, numerical estimates if reported, and study limitations. Search for phrases such as non-Asian women, historical HBV DNA, quantitative HBsAg, cirrhosis.'}

The directly relevant clinical study was a retrospective cohort of **119 asymptomatic, treatment-naïve non-Asian women with chronic hepatitis B**. Historic serum samples were collected during pregnancy in 1990–2004 and compared with samples collected in 2011–2012 (median interval 17 years; IQR 13–20). Liver stiffness measurement classified 14 women (12%) as F3–F4 at a threshold of >8.1 kPa; this was an elastography-defined prevalent outcome, not biopsy-confirmed cirrhosis.

**Adjusted associations:** Neither HBV DNA nor quantitative HBsAg was an independent predictor. Historic HBV DNA had a reported RR of **0.34 (95% CI 0.05–2.44)**, and qHBsAg >1,000 IU/mL had an RR of **0.35 (95% CI 0.11–1.11)**—neither statistically significant. The abstract provides no separate numerical estimate for current HBV DNA or current qHBsAg. Alcohol use (OR **6.4**, 95% CI 1.3–30.1), AST >0.5×ULN (OR **15.4**, 95% CI 1.9–122.6), and prothrombin time (OR **12.0**, 95% CI 1.2–120.4) were reported as independent predictors.

**Limitations:** Only 14 participants met the outcome definition, and the estimates were imprecise. The retrospective design and LSM-based F3–F4 classification limit conclusions about biopsy-proven cirrhosis and future risk. The available abstract does not report numerical adjusted estimates for current viral markers, and full text was unavailable to verify further limitations. The null findings should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

In the directly relevant study, a retrospective cohort of 119 non-Asian women with chronic hepatitis B was assessed for advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis by liver stiffness measurement. Neither historical nor current HBV DNA nor quantitative HBsAg was reported as an independent predictor. The reported estimates included historical HBV DNA (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.05–2.44) and qHBsAg >1,000 IU/mL (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.11–1.11), both statistically nonsignificant.

Interpret this as **no association detected**, not proof that no association exists: only 14 women met the elastography-defined F3–F4 outcome, estimates were imprecise, and the outcome was not biopsy-confirmed cirrhosis. The abstract did not provide separate numerical estimates for current HBV DNA or current qHBsAg.

FINAL DECISION: NO
